children.text: T2: Mechanical accelerator

A massless thread makes \(N\) turns around a statically fixed cylinder, as shown in the figure. Initially, the free (unwound) ends of the thread are parallel to the axis \(X\). Then, a heavy point-like object \(P\) is attached to one end of the thread while the other end is pulled with a constant velocity \(u\) along \(X\). Find the maximum velocity attained by the heavy object.

nodes.alt: Original apparatus: a thread makes N tight turns around a fixed cylinder. A point mass P is attached to its left end and the other end is pulled to the right at constant speed u along X.

children.text: The thread is inextensible and flexible. Suppose that the turns of the thread are wound tightly to one another and are placed practically in the same plane, perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Neglect any friction in the system. Do not consider the force of gravity.

statement.text:
T2: Mechanical accelerator
A massless thread makes \(N\) turns around a statically fixed cylinder, as shown in the figure. Initially, the free (unwound) ends of the thread are parallel to the axis \(X\). Then, a heavy point-like object \(P\) is attached to one end of the thread while the other end is pulled with a constant velocity \(u\) along \(X\). Find the maximum velocity attained by the heavy object.

The thread is inextensible and flexible. Suppose that the turns of the thread are wound tightly to one another and are placed practically in the same plane, perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Neglect any friction in the system. Do not consider the force of gravity.

children.text: T2: Mechanical accelerator

nodes.alt: Original solution diagrams: Earth-frame longitudinal and transverse velocity components at P and thread angle phi, alongside a frame rotating about the cylinder with P, Q, radius R and unwound length l_P.

children.text: Solution I: rotating basis along the thread

Resolve the velocity into a longitudinal component along the thread and a transverse component. Let \(\mathbf e_1\) point from the cylinder toward \(P\), \(\mathbf e_2\) be perpendicular to it, and \(\varphi\) be the total turning angle measured from the initial thread direction. Inextensibility fixes \(v_l=-u\).
\[\mathbf v=-u\mathbf e_1+v_\perp\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_1=\dot\varphi\mathbf e_2,\qquad \dot{\mathbf e}_2=-\dot\varphi\mathbf e_1.\]
\[\mathbf a=-v_\perp\dot\varphi\mathbf e_1+(\dot v_\perp-u\dot\varphi)\mathbf e_2.\]
Tension is the only force and acts along the thread, so the perpendicular acceleration vanishes. Starting with zero transverse velocity gives
\[\dot v_\perp=u\dot\varphi,\qquad v_\perp=u\varphi.\]
At complete detachment, the thread has turned through \(2\pi N\). Hence
\[v_\perp=2\pi Nu,\qquad v_{\rm detach}=u\sqrt{1+(2\pi N)^2}.\]

Detachment does not give the maximum laboratory speed. After detachment, use the inertial frame translating with the pulled end at speed \(u\). The mass rotates around that end at constant relative speed \(2\pi Nu\), because tension does no work in that frame. The laboratory speed is maximal when the relative velocity points in the pulling direction, with the thread perpendicular to \(X\).
Solution II: a rotating reference frame

Let \(R\) be the cylinder radius and choose a frame rotating at \(\omega=u/R\). The wound thread is at rest in this frame. A point \(Q\) on the pulled end rotates relative to the cylinder with angular velocity \(-\omega\). The mass moves perpendicular to its unwound thread, so tension does no work in this frame. Coriolis force also does no work. Its kinetic-energy gain equals its loss of centrifugal potential energy.
\[\frac12mv_P^2=-\frac12m\omega^2R^2+\frac12m\omega^2r^2=\frac12m\omega^2l_P^2,\qquad v_P=\frac uR l_P,\qquad \omega_P=\frac{v_P}{l_P}=\omega.\]

Here \(r\) is the distance from the cylinder axis to \(P\) and \(l_P\) is its unwound thread length. The ends unwind symmetrically in the rotating frame, so their straight lengths are equal. At detachment,
\[l_P=\pi NR,\qquad v_P=\pi Nu.\]

Adding the rotating-frame velocity to \(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r\) gives the laboratory transverse component \(v_\perp=2v_P=2\pi Nu\). Continue in the translating frame after detachment as in Solution I to obtain \(v_{\max}=u(2\pi N+1)\).
Solution III: work and energy
Again \(v_l=-u\). The longitudinal acceleration is \(-v_\perp\dot\varphi\). If \(F\) denotes the signed longitudinal component of the tension, Newton's law and the work-energy theorem give
\[F=-mv_\perp\dot\varphi,\qquad \frac{dE_k}{dt}=Fv_l=mv_\perp\dot\varphi u,\qquad E_k=\frac12m(u^2+v_\perp^2).\]

Differentiating the last expression gives \(\dot v_\perp=u\dot\varphi\). The remainder is identical to Solution I. The signed \(F\) is negative because the actual tension points toward the cylinder, opposite to \(\mathbf e_1\).
